title: What the Song of Songs Really Celebrates
paragraphs:
What the Song of Songs Really Celebrates
The Bible’s Most Intimate Book Is Not About Lust. It Is About Love Without Shame—and the God Who Refuses to Let Desire Become Our God.
There is a book in your Bible that some Christians almost seem embarrassed to read out loud.
It talks about kisses.
Longing.
Beauty.
Bodies.
Fragrance.
Desire.
A man looking at a woman and being overwhelmed by her beauty.
A woman longing for the man she loves.

There are gardens, perfumes, embraces, anticipation, separation, pursuit, exclusivity, vulnerability, and words so intimate that if you did not already know they were Scripture, you might be surprised to discover they were sitting between Ecclesiastes and Isaiah.
And perhaps that discomfort tells us something.
Maybe we have spent so much time hearing the world distort desire that we have forgotten God created desire before sin ever corrupted it.
Maybe some Christians have become so afraid of lust that we have accidentally become suspicious of beauty.
Maybe others have swallowed the opposite lie—that because desire is natural, every desire must therefore be obeyed.
Song of Songs refuses both lies.
It does not tell us the body is dirty.
And it does not tell us desire is sovereign.
Instead, it gives us something far more beautiful:

desire redeemed by covenant, passion restrained by wisdom, bodies treated with dignity, longing joined to faithfulness, and love so powerful that Scripture eventually compares it to fire and death itself.
The Hebrew title announces what kind of song we are entering:
שִׁיר הַשִּׁירִים — Shir haShirim
Literally, “Song of Songs.”
Hebrew sometimes uses this kind of construction to express supremacy. “Holy of holies” means the most holy. “King of kings” means the supreme king.
So “Song of Songs” presents itself as a song above songs.
And its opening does not sound embarrassed:
יִשָּׁקֵנִי מִנְּשִׁיקוֹת פִּיהוּ
Yishaqeni minneshiqot pihu.

“Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth…”
—Song of Songs 1:2
Notice who speaks.
The woman.
That matters.
Biblical love is not portrayed here as a woman existing merely as an object for male appetite. She speaks. She desires. She searches. She praises. She chooses her words. She expresses longing.
And the man does not merely consume her beauty.
He beholds it.
He praises her.
Again and again, they speak to one another rather than merely taking from one another.
“My beloved is mine, and I am his” becomes one of the Song’s recurring declarations of mutual belonging.
That is worlds apart from pornography.
Pornography says, “Your body exists for my consumption.”
Lust says, “I want what I want from you.”
Predatory desire asks, “How much can I take?”
The Song asks something radically different:
How deeply can love delight without degrading?
How passionately can two people desire without turning one another into objects?
How can the body be celebrated without becoming an idol?
How can longing remain beautiful instead of becoming destructive?
And then comes one of the most important warnings in the entire book.
Not once.
Repeatedly.
אַל־תָּעִירוּ וְאַל־תְּעוֹרְרוּ אֶת־הָאַהֲבָה עַד שֶׁתֶּחְפָּץ
Al-ta'iru ve'al-te'oreru et-ha'ahavah ad shetechpatz.
Do not stir up or awaken love until it pleases.
The warning appears in Song of Songs 2:7, 3:5, and again in 8:4 with slightly varied wording.
Why would a book celebrating desire repeatedly tell us not to awaken it prematurely?
Because the Bible understands something our culture desperately needs to remember.
Powerful things require boundaries.
Fire can warm a home.
Fire can also burn one down.
Water can sustain life.
Water can also drown it.
Sexual desire is not evil because it is powerful.
Its power is precisely why wisdom matters.
The Song never treats passion casually.
That may be one of its most startling messages to a culture drowning in casual intimacy.
We have been taught to separate bodies from covenant, pleasure from permanence, sex from sacred responsibility, attraction from character, and intimacy from consequences.
Then we wonder why so many people feel used.
Why they feel discarded.
Why they can share a bed yet remain terrified of sharing their heart.
Why people who have been touched everywhere can still feel completely unknown.
Why someone can have hundreds of digital admirers and still lie awake wondering whether anybody would remain if they saw the whole truth.
The Song celebrates something different.
Not merely being wanted.
Being cherished.
Not merely chemistry.
Faithfulness.
Not merely nakedness.
Safety.
Not merely attraction.
Belonging.
This is why reducing Song of Songs to “the Bible's book about sex” misses so much.
Yes, the poetry is sensual.

Christian interpreters should not sanitize what Scripture itself does not sanitize. Serious interpreters widely recognize that the Song genuinely celebrates human romantic and sexual love. Yet the poetry also displays notable restraint: it celebrates the body without becoming pornography, and its repeated warnings against prematurely awakening love place desire under wisdom rather than enthroning desire as master.
The Song is not ashamed of sexuality.
But neither does it worship sexuality.
And that distinction may expose one of the deepest wounds of our generation.
Some of us were taught that sex was dirty.
Others were taught that sex was everything.
Jesus rescues us from both lies.
The body is not dirty.
The body was created by God.
Genesis tells us that humanity was created male and female in God's image, and before shame entered the human story, the man and woman could be naked without shame.
Then came the serpent.
Then rebellion.
Then hiding.
That sequence matters.
Shame was not God's original wedding gift.
It entered after sin.
Humanity took something God called good and dragged it through rebellion, domination, exploitation, adultery, abuse, selfishness, lust, abandonment, pornography, manipulation, and heartbreak.
And perhaps that is why this book can hurt while it heals.
Because some people reading this do not associate romance with gardens.
You associate it with betrayal.
You remember the message you discovered.
The secret account.
The affair.
The person who promised forever and disappeared when forever became inconvenient.
You remember giving your body because you were afraid saying no would make them leave.
You remember confusing attention with love.
You remember lowering convictions because loneliness was louder than wisdom.
Maybe nobody forced you.
Maybe you simply knew better and did it anyway.
And afterward came that horrible silence.
That moment when temptation had already collected its payment but never delivered what it promised.
Some sins scream before we commit them.
Sexual sin often whispers before and screams afterward.
“What have I done?”
And perhaps you have carried that question for years.
Listen carefully.
Song of Songs celebrates holy love.
But the Gospel announces something even more astonishing for people whose stories have not been holy.
Jesus Christ does not only receive people who preserved perfect histories.
He redeems sinners.
That is why the Christian message cannot end with “Try harder to become pure.”
If purity depended upon an untouched past, millions of people would have no hope.
But Christianity is built around a Savior who makes the unclean clean.

At the cross, Jesus did not die for an imaginary collection of people who had never crossed boundaries, never lusted, never cheated, never used another person, never been used, never awakened love foolishly, never watched what they should not have watched, never entered the wrong bedroom, never broken a vow.
“Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners” (1 Timothy 1:15).
Sinners.
People with histories.
People with screenshots they wish never existed.
People with relationships they wish they could erase.
People who betrayed spouses.
People who were betrayed.
People who crossed lines.
People whose lines were violated.
People who spent years calling bondage freedom.
People who finally discovered that getting what they wanted could not heal what was broken inside them.
The answer is not pretending sin does not matter.
Grace is not God shrugging at rebellion.
Jesus' call includes repentance.
Turn.
Come into the light.
Stop defending what is destroying you.
Confess what you have hidden.
Bring your sexuality under the lordship of Christ.
Receive forgiveness that you could never manufacture for yourself.
Because the scandal of Christianity is not that sin is insignificant.
The scandal is that the Son of God willingly bore judgment for sinners who could never cleanse themselves.
And then Song of Songs brings us to its blazing summit:
כִּי־עַזָּה כַמָּוֶת אַהֲבָה
Ki-azzah khamavet ahavah.
“For love is strong as death.”
Then:
רְשָׁפֶיהָ רִשְׁפֵּי אֵשׁ שַׁלְהֶבֶתְיָה
Its flashes are flashes of fire—a mighty flame.
—Song of Songs 8:6

The final Hebrew expression, שַׁלְהֶבֶתְיָה — shalhevetyah, is famously striking. It can be understood as an intensely powerful flame, and many translations and interpreters understand the ending -yah as invoking the divine name: “the flame of the LORD.”
Either way, the image is enormous.
Love burns.
Love costs.
Love binds.
Love cannot simply be purchased.
The next verse says that many waters cannot quench love and floods cannot drown it. It adds that if someone attempted to buy love with all the wealth of his house, he would be utterly despised.
You can buy sex.
You cannot buy love.
You can buy attention.
You cannot buy faithfulness.
You can purchase an image designed to imitate intimacy.
You cannot purchase covenant.
You can manipulate someone into remaining physically present.
You cannot manufacture genuine devotion.
Real love refuses to become merchandise.
And suddenly the Song begins speaking directly into the marketplace of modern loneliness.
Swipe.
Consume.
Compare.
Discard.
Repeat.
Always another face.
Always another fantasy.
Always another possibility.
Always the suggestion that perhaps happiness is one more person away.
But Scripture keeps whispering:
Love is not a product.
A human being is not content.
A body is not merchandise.
And desire makes a terrible god.
This is also where Christians must be careful with the Song.

For centuries, Jewish and Christian interpreters frequently read it allegorically as God's love for Israel or Christ's love for His Church. Modern interpreters have rightly emphasized its plain sense as poetry celebrating human love. We do not need to mutilate either truth to honor Christ.
The Song should first be allowed to speak as the remarkable biblical celebration of human love that it is.
Then we read it inside the whole canon of Scripture.
And there we discover something breathtaking.
Marriage itself ultimately points beyond itself.
Paul writes concerning husband and wife in Ephesians 5 and then says:
“This mystery is profound, and I am saying that it refers to Christ and the church.”
Marriage is not Jesus.
Romantic love is not Jesus.
Sex is not Jesus.
A spouse cannot save you.
That may sound obvious until you watch how desperately human beings ask romance to do what only God can do.
“Tell me I matter.”
“Make me whole.”
“Never disappoint me.”
“Never leave me emotionally hungry.”
“Give my life meaning.”
“Fix my loneliness.”
“Convince me I am worthy.”
No husband can carry that weight.
No wife can carry that weight.
No boyfriend.
No girlfriend.
No wedding.
No sexual experience.
Created love is beautiful precisely because it does not have to become God.
And for the single Christian, this matters enormously.
Song of Songs is not telling you that you are half a human being until somebody desires you romantically.
Jesus Himself lived the perfect human life without marriage.
Paul could speak positively of singleness in 1 Corinthians 7.
Your marital status does not determine your spiritual completeness.
Christ does.
Human marriage is temporary.
The marriage toward which history itself is moving is eternal.
Revelation does not end with humanity finally discovering better dating.
It ends with a wedding.
The Bridegroom.
Christ.
His redeemed people.
The marriage supper of the Lamb.
And here the beauty of Song of Songs begins opening toward something greater than itself.
Every faithful marriage whispers that covenant matters.
Every husband who sacrifices instead of exploiting whispers something about Christ.
Every wife cherished rather than consumed reminds us that biblical love recognizes dignity.
Every act of forgiveness inside a wounded marriage whispers that grace can enter places pride wanted to bury.
Every couple choosing fidelity when temptation says “Nobody will know” declares that love is more than appetite.
Yet every human marriage eventually confronts its limits.
Bodies age.
Beauty changes.
Hands wrinkle.
Desire passes through seasons.
Illness comes.
Death separates.
The lovers of Song of Songs can say love is strong as death.
The Gospel goes further.
Jesus Christ entered death…
and came back.
That changes everything.
The greatest love story in Scripture is ultimately not humanity climbing toward God.
It is God coming after rebels.
Christ did not wait for His Bride to make herself worthy before loving her.
He gave Himself for her.
He cleanses.
He sanctifies.
He restores.
He makes beautiful what sin had stained.
And that means your story does not have to end where your worst chapter happened.
Maybe your scandal was sexual.
Maybe it was adultery.
Pornography.
Secret messages.
Emotional infidelity.
Sex outside marriage.
A relationship you knew dishonored God.
Maybe nobody knows.
Maybe everybody knows.
Maybe your scandal was not something you chose but something another person did to you, leaving you with wounds you still struggle to name.
Jesus does not confuse what was done against you with what you willingly did.
And neither should the Church.
But whether you need forgiveness for sin you committed or healing from evil committed against you, the invitation leads toward the same Savior.
Jesus Christ.
There is grace here.
Not cheap grace that tells you to continue destroying yourself.
Transforming grace.
Grace that forgives and then teaches you to walk differently.
Grace that can teach a husband to look at his wife again with tenderness instead of entitlement.
Grace that can teach a wife that her worth was never dependent upon comparison.
Grace that can teach a teenager that waiting is not weakness.
Grace that can teach the lonely that loneliness does not justify disobedience.
Grace that can lead the addicted into confession.
Grace that can lead the adulterer into repentance.
Grace that can lead a wounded marriage toward truth.
Grace that can teach a generation raised on pornography how to see human beings as image-bearers again.
This is what Song of Songs really celebrates.
Not lust.
Not promiscuity.
Not bodies detached from souls.
Not desire without boundaries.
It celebrates the astonishing goodness of embodied, faithful, exclusive human love under the wisdom of God.
It tells us desire is powerful enough that we should not awaken it carelessly.
It tells us genuine love cannot be bought.
It tells us the body can be spoken about without shame and admired without degradation.
It reminds married believers that delight in one's spouse is not spiritually inferior simply because it is physical.
And within the full story of Scripture, marriage itself becomes a signpost pointing beyond every earthly lover toward Christ and His redeemed Bride.
So perhaps the question is no longer merely, “What does Song of Songs mean?”
Perhaps the more dangerous question is:
What has been teaching you how to love?
Pornography?
TikTok?
Movies?
Your wounds?
Your hormones?
Your loneliness?
Your parents' broken marriage?
The person who abandoned you?
The culture?
Or the God who invented love before the world learned how to counterfeit it?
Be honest.
Some of us do not need another relationship.
We need repentance.
Some do not need another dating app.
We need healing.
Some married couples do not need a newer partner.
They need renewed covenant faithfulness.
Some singles do not need to lower their standards because the waiting hurts.
They need to remember that awakening love before its proper time can create wounds desperation never warned them about.
And some of you need to stop believing your past has disqualified you from ever becoming clean.
If Christ has forgiven you, stop digging through the graveyard looking for the person He buried.
Walk in repentance.
Walk in purity.
Walk in grace.
And when you fall, do not run deeper into darkness.
Run toward Jesus.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not have to describe your private sin publicly. But you can comment, “Jesus, make my heart clean.”
If you are fighting to honor Christ with your body and relationships, comment, “I’m still fighting.”
If your marriage needs prayer, simply comment, “Pray for us.”

And if Christ is restoring an area of your life you once thought was beyond redemption, comment, “Christ is still healing me.” Your testimony may become the reason another ashamed believer finally realizes that repentance is not the end of the story.
Not because every sentence will be easy to hear, but because there may come a night when desire becomes louder than wisdom and you need to remember:
Do not awaken love before its time.

Supporting Gospel work should never be presented as purchasing God's favor or proving that you glorify Him—salvation is by grace, not payment. But generous support can genuinely help biblical teaching reach people who may never walk into a church.
Invite your family.
Invite the struggling believer.
Invite the person who walked away from church.
Invite the Christian who has grown lukewarm.
Invite the seeker.
Even invite the unbelieving friend who thinks Christianity only knows how to shame human desire.
Let them encounter the Bible for themselves.
Because Song of Songs does not reveal a God embarrassed by love.
It reveals a God wise enough to know that something this powerful must never be treated cheaply.

And maybe tonight, after all the Hebrew words, ancient poetry, gardens, kisses, warnings, fire, longing, covenant, failure, repentance, and grace, only one sentence needs to remain burning in your memory:
Your desires do not get to write the ending—Jesus does.
